name: Handshake
brief: Setup is complete and you're ready for action.
tech: A handshake is the exchange that two systems use to establish a working connection. Once it completes, the actual work can begin.
situation: A new agreement is in place between two parties.
examples: Starting a new job
Making a relationship official
Signing a contract
Joining a team or partnership
Initiating a creative collaboration
reflection: A handshake is the multi-step exchange by which two systems confirm they can communicate and on what terms. Each side signals readiness, and the protocol completes only when both confirm. From this point forward, both are bound to what was agreed. The most visible part of a handshake is the connection, but the terms affect everything that follows.

name: Bridge
brief: A bridge between two worlds.
tech: A network bridge connects two network segments so traffic flows between them. More broadly, a bridge links two systems built on different terms.
situation: You are the connection between two or more separate worlds.
examples: Translating between two people who think very differently
Helping a partner understand your family or vice versa
Explaining a job to people outside the field
Mediating a conflict
Connecting friends with coworkers
reflection: A bridge is the structural element that allows two different systems to interact. Each side communicates in its own way. To translate, the bridge has to understand both of their ways at once. Neither endpoint does this. From the middle, the bridge can see things about each side that the sides cannot see about themselves.

name: Loopback
brief: You are in conversation with yourself.
tech: Loopback is when a system communicates with itself. It is often used for testing, or for two programs on the same machine to talk to each other.
situation: You are working through something on your own.
examples: Rehearsing a conversation in your head
Revising an unsent message
Ruminating on something that happened
Imagining what someone would say
Wavering on a decision
reflection: A loopback routes a signal from a system back to itself. Outputs become the next inputs, and no new information enters from outside. Closed loops are sometimes deliberate, used for calibration, self-test, or internal processing. They can also serve as a stand-in for the exchange that would actually resolve the situation. Without an external point of reference, it can be difficult to tell the difference.

name: Echo
brief: Whatever you put out comes back to you unchanged.
tech: An echo is the return of a signal in the same form it was sent.
situation: The same patterns keep returning.
examples: Repeating the same pattern in successive relationships
Finding yourself acting just like your parents
Saying the same thing and getting the same response
Encountering the same problems everywhere you go
Surrounding yourself with people who think just like you
reflection: An echo is the return of a signal in the same form it was sent. The system sends, the same form returns, and over time the pattern repeats. When everything that comes back matches what was sent, the loop has closed to outside input. Confirmation that arrives from a closed loop is structurally indistinguishable from no information. A system that only hears its own signal cannot detect when it has drifted from reality.

name: Static
brief: What you're trying to hear or say is getting lost in too much noise.
tech: Static is random noise that gets mixed into a transmission and makes the actual signal hard to hear.
situation: Too much noise obscures what matters.
examples: Trying to focus while notifications keep going off
Having a serious conversation in a busy public place
Making yourself heard in a loud group
Trying to choose what you want from too many options
Thinking clearly when your mind is full of noise
reflection: Static is noise mixed into a transmission that makes the actual signal hard to hear. The signal is still present. Multiple sources contribute noise to the channel at once, and at some point the signal-to-noise ratio crosses a threshold where the message becomes inaudible. Recovery happens by reducing noise or strengthening signal. Most of the time, the message hasn't disappeared.

name: Connection Refused
brief: You got an answer, and the answer was no.
tech: Connection Refused is a specific TCP error. The rejection is clear, immediate, and definitive.
situation: A direct, unambiguous no.
examples: A job application denied
An invitation declined
A breakup
A block on social media
A rejection from a romantic interest
reflection: Connection Refused is the case where the destination is reachable and responsive but actively rejects the request. The rejection itself is a signal. The system is functioning and the answer has been delivered. Unlike silence or unreachability, the situation contains no ambiguity. A clear refusal closes a possibility with certainty. Even when it isn't what you wanted to hear, at least you're not left wondering.

name: Idle
brief: You have time and capacity, and nothing is required of you.
tech: Idle is when a system has capacity available with nothing currently using it.
situation: Free time with no demands.
examples: A vacation
An evening with no obligations
A pause between projects
An open Saturday afternoon
Rest after hard work
reflection: Idle is when a system has capacity available with nothing currently using it. The system is fully operational, with no active demand. Capacity is present and uncalled. The state can be mistaken for malfunction by anyone who measures function by activity, but the system is working correctly.

name: Throttled
brief: You're holding something back.
tech: Throttling is when a system intentionally limits the rate of output.
situation: Not fully sharing everything that you could.
examples: Hiding aspects of yourself while at work
Working at a slower speed to avoid overwhelming someone
Not voicing your creative ideas
Speaking carefully to avoid conflict
Editing yourself to avoid offending others
reflection: Throttling is when a system intentionally limits the rate of its output. The full capacity remains present. The constraint is structural, set somewhere in the configuration. A throttle exists for a reason: protecting downstream systems, conserving resources, meeting external rules. The constraint can outlast the conditions that produced it. A throttle that goes unexamined becomes invisible. Over time, the limit can stop being recognized as something you can change. It may begin to feel like the actual bounds of what is possible.

name: Buffer Full
brief: You're already at your limit, and more keeps adding pressure.
tech: A buffer is temporary storage that holds data while it's moving from one place to another.
situation: Everything pressing on you at once.
examples: Drowning in unread messages
Falling behind on a growing todo list
Juggling too many commitments at once
Treating everything coming in as urgent
Running from one thing to the next without a break
reflection: The system is at capacity. Inputs are arriving faster than they can be processed, and every system at this point either drops new input, queues it indefinitely, or applies backpressure to the source. There is no fourth option. The choice is being made now, with or without your awareness or consent.

name: Stale Cache
brief: You're working from outdated information.
tech: A cache stores a copy of data so it can be retrieved quickly without going back to the original source.
situation: Going by what used to be true.
examples: Treating someone as the person they used to be
Returning to a place expecting it to be unchanged
Keeping an outdated self-image
Not seeing that a relationship has changed
Going by social rules that have since evolved
Holding on to opinions you formed long ago
reflection: A cache holds a copy of data taken at some point in the past. The system reads from the cache rather than the source, which is cheaper and faster. The cache becomes stale when the source changes but the copy stays the same. From inside the system, there is no automatic signal that the cache has gone stale. The system continues operating on the snapshot, producing results that are internally consistent and externally wrong. The cache cannot detect its own staleness. Only external validation reveals what is still true.

name: Memory Leak
brief: Something is draining your attention.
tech: A memory leak is when a program holds onto memory past when it needs it.
situation: Something keeps bothering you.
examples: A recurring worry
A frequent regret
An unprocessed loss
A relived trauma
A nagging health issue
reflection: A memory leak is when a system holds onto information past when it needs it. Each instance is small. Their accumulation, over time, becomes the structural issue. Slow leaks are difficult to detect in the moment because the system continues running and capacity decreases gradually. But the effect is noticeable: the system feels heavier, slower, or less responsive, without anything specific being clearly wrong.

name: Crash
brief: Something has suddenly stopped, and is now gone.
tech: A crash is when a system stops running suddenly because of an error that broke it.
situation: A sudden ending.
examples: A relationship that ended
A sudden loss in the family
An unexpected health crisis
A job or career ending abruptly
A mental or emotional breakdown
reflection: A crash is when a system stops running suddenly. State held in memory at the time of the break is lost. In computing, state written to durable storage survives, and the system can be restarted from it. In life, what is lost often cannot be restored. You move forward, changed by both what is gone and what remains.

name: Heartbeat
brief: A steady rhythm that keeps something alive.
tech: A heartbeat is a regular signal sent at fixed intervals so other systems know a process is still alive.
situation: Small steady actions that maintain something.
examples: Calling your parents every week
Going to therapy even when you feel fine
Following a daily routine
Walking the dog every morning
Tending to the basics of food, sleep, and movement
reflection: A heartbeat is a regular signal sent at fixed intervals to indicate a system is still alive. Other systems listen for the steady rhythm to know the sender is alive. When the rhythm stops, the sender is presumed failed. Sustained over time, the beats become a meaningful pattern.

name: Sync
brief: Things working together to make something possible.
tech: Sync is when two or more systems align in time so their actions happen together, or they reach the same state at once.
situation: Independent things aligning into coordinated action.
examples: A team working together effectively
A creative breakthrough from collaboration
Two people hitting it off on first meeting
An event coming together
Being on the same wavelength with someone else
reflection: Synchronization is the alignment of multiple systems in time so their actions or states coincide. Most systems run on independent rhythms. Sync is the rare condition where those rhythms briefly come into phase. When it happens, coordinated action becomes possible that no system could produce alone.

name: Polling
brief: You keep checking for something that hasn't happened yet.
tech: Polling is when a system repeatedly checks for an update at regular intervals.
situation: Repeatedly checking while you wait.
examples: Reloading your inbox waiting for a reply
Checking your phone repeatedly for a text
Watching for news of a pending event
Checking the mail for an expected package
Watching the door for someone to arrive
reflection: Polling is the pattern of repeatedly checking for an update at fixed intervals. Each check returns the current state, whether or not anything has changed. When checking happens faster than the change, most checks find nothing new. What polling reliably gives the watcher is something to do and a feeling of agency.

name: Latency
brief: There's a long wait between your input and the response.
tech: Latency is the delay between when something is sent and when it arrives.
situation: Time passing between cause and effect.
examples: A message you sent that hasn't been answered yet
A decision whose consequences are still undetermined
A career move that hasn't paid off so far
A new habit that hasn't changed your life yet
A medical treatment that takes weeks to start working
reflection: Latency is the delay between when a signal is sent and when it arrives. During this time, the signal is in transit. No information about the result is available until the transmission has finished. The temptation during latency is to interpret the message before it is received. A signal in transit is not yet a result. Whatever finally arrives might be very different from what you imagined.

name: Timeout
brief: You waited for a response that never arrived.
tech: A timeout is when a system gives up waiting for a response. After a configured time, the request is treated as failed.
situation: Silence where an answer was expected.
examples: A job application that goes unanswered
A date request that gets ignored
A friendship that fades away
A promise that never gets fulfilled
An apology that never comes
reflection: A timeout is the moment a system stops waiting for a response that never came. The request was sent, a window of time passed, and no answer arrived. The other side might never have received the message, or might have received it and chosen not to reply. From this side, both look the same. A timeout is structurally ambiguous: it only tells you that nothing came back. Choosing to time out is a choice to stop waiting. Why no response came may never be known.

name: Deadlock
brief: Both sides are stuck, each waiting for the other to make the first move.
tech: A deadlock is when two or more processes are each waiting for the other to release something.
situation: Two sides waiting for the other to take action.
examples: After an argument, friends waiting for each other to apologize
Two cars at an intersection, each waiting for the other to move first
A negotiation frozen with both sides waiting for the other to budge
Two people interested in each other, both waiting for the other to make a move
A meeting where no one wants to be the first to speak
reflection: A deadlock is when two or more sides each wait for the other to make the first move. As long as both wait, both stay stuck. The freeze ends when someone acts.

name: Patch
brief: A quick fix to keep things going for now.
tech: A patch is a small, quick change made to fix a specific problem.
situation: A temporary fix.
examples: Patching a flat tire
Taking medicine for symptoms until you can determine the cause
Negotiating a temporary work arrangement
Apologizing to quickly end a conflict
Borrowing money to cover an unexpected expense
reflection: A patch is a small, localized change that fixes a specific problem without altering the underlying structure. The symptom goes away and the system runs again. Patches keep things going, but they accumulate, and a system covered in patches becomes harder to understand and harder to repair properly. Applying a patch can give you the time to design a proper fix.

name: Branch
brief: You face a decision.
tech: A branch is a divergent line of development that splits off from the main one.
situation: Weighing options before deciding.
examples: Keeping your current job or accepting a new offer
Committing to a relationship or remaining single
Speaking up about something or keeping it to yourself
Staying close to family or moving far away
Doing what you really want or what is expected of you
reflection: A branch is a divergent line of development that splits off from the main one. At a branching point, you can't fully know how each option will actually play out. You decide anyway, and the consequences follow over time.

name: Merge
brief: Two separate things are coming together.
tech: A merge is when two separate branches of work are combined into one.
situation: Separate streams joining.
examples: Reconnecting with a partner after time apart
Combining two separate work projects into one
Integrating your personal and professional lives
Moving in together
Two families becoming one
reflection: A merge is when two separate things become one. Becoming one changes both sides. The merged result is something that contains elements of both, but is also something new.

name: Garbage Collection
brief: Releasing what has served its purpose.
tech: Garbage collection is the automatic process by which a system reclaims memory that is no longer useful. The reclaimed space becomes available for new work.
situation: Time to clear out what is finished.
examples: Letting go of an old grudge
Giving away clothes you haven't worn in years
Quitting a habit you've outgrown
Releasing a friendship that's run its course
Donating books you've already read
reflection: Garbage collection is the process by which a system reclaims memory that nothing active still uses. Without periodic clearing, capacity stays committed to things that have already served their purpose. In computing, this clearing happens automatically. In life, the same work has to be done deliberately.

name: Upgrade
brief: You're upgrading something.
tech: An upgrade replaces a system with a newer version that has more capabilities or improvements.
situation: Replacing the old with something better.
examples: Getting better at something through practice
Moving into a home that better fits your needs
A new car that's more reliable
Stepping into a more challenging role
Personal growth from therapy
reflection: An upgrade replaces a system with a newer version that can do more. In computing, the upgrade is installed all at once. In life, it happens gradually, through what you experience and the work you put in.

name: Reset
brief: You are starting over.
tech: A reset returns a system to its starting state.
situation: A fresh start.
examples: Starting over after a major life change
Picking up the pieces after a relationship ends
Going back to school as an adult
Changing jobs or careers
Moving to a new home
reflection: A reset clears whatever has accumulated. Variables, configuration, working memory, all of it is wiped. In computing, the system returns to its original initial conditions. In life, a reset rarely returns you to exactly who you were before, as everything you've been through stays with you.
